Corporate Finance Research Assistant

A hands-on tutorial: link PSID children to their mothers with SQL inside Python, build three decades of income histories with JOIN and GROUP BY, and estimate how strongly income persists across generations. Daughters and sons tell different stories, and one year of income, or one measured too early, can badly mislead.


BLOG 5 Why a Tech-Rich State Can Still Have a Wide Gender Pay Gap Claudia Goldin’s research frames a deeper look at gender earnings across 50 states: who holds the technology jobs, what women and men earn inside tech, and why prosperity alone does not close the gap. Census maps and trends from 2019 to 2024 connect access, pay, and the cost of flexibility.


BLOG 4 More Tech, Better Jobs? Does a growing technology workforce mean a stronger job market? Census data across 50 states and six years reveal that rising tech employment shares did not consistently accompany lower unemployment or higher employment rates. Four charts and two U.S. maps compare states, track changes over time, and take a closer look at two Bay Area core counties.


BLOG 3 How Much of the Participation Decline Reflects an Aging Population? A falling national average can hide a changing population. Using more than two million weighted CPS person-month observations, this post separates the 2019–2024 decline in labor-force participation into age composition and changes within age groups. Three charts show how an aging population outweighed participation gains—and why the headline rate cannot tell the whole story.


BLOG 2 What Is Your Student ID Worth? Where does a student ID save the most—and where can you visit for less? Using R to collect official admission prices, this post compares 18 museums across eight U.S. cities. Philadelphia offers the largest average student discount in this sample, but museums that are free for everyone tell a different story about affordability. title: What Is Your Student ID Worth?
text:
What does student status save?
How much does being a student reduce the cost of visiting a museum? I collected posted admission prices for 18 museums in eight U.S. cities, comparing what a student and a nonstudent of the same age would pay. This separates the discount attached to student status from the price of the visit itself: a large discount may still leave an expensive ticket, while a museum that is free to everyone offers no additional saving for students.

title: What Is Your Student ID Worth?
text:
Building a comparable ticket
I screened 30 institutions and retained 18 with extractable, comparable prices across 8 cities. This is a convenience sample, mostly art museums, not a representative survey. One institution contributes one observation; multiple buildings and repeated daily price tables do not become extra museums.
The baseline compares a 30-year-old, nonresident, full-time college student with valid ID against an otherwise equivalent nonstudent. Age 30 separates student status from youth eligibility; a second view uses age 22. Penn-specific partnerships, resident discounts, memberships, transportation, parking, booking fees, and separately ticketed exhibitions are excluded. Results describe posted general-admission prices, not a complete travel budget.
Student-ID saving = comparable adult price − student price.
Using R’s rvest, I parsed cached official HTML with read_html(), html_elements(), and html_text2(). Site-specific category patterns distinguish student tickets from parking charges and nonresident rates from local offers. Missing categories stop the analysis; missing prices never become zero. Short evidence extracts, source URLs, collection logs, and scripts accompany the cleaned data.
Requests were spaced and cached. Access refusals, rate limits, robot exclusions, and challenge pages were not bypassed. Barnes and The Broad were dropped after reviewing restrictive terms. This matters statistically: websites that are easier to read can become overrepresented.

title: What Is Your Student ID Worth?
text:
Where the card saves more



Philadelphia has the largest average posted student discount in this selected sample; each city label shows its sample size.


Philadelphia leads this sample at $12.75 per museum, compared with $9.50 in New York. Visiting all four sampled Philadelphia institutions once would cost $42.00 using student rates, versus $93.00 at adult rates. This is a basket calculation, not a one-day itinerary.
To summarize the regional pattern, I give each sampled city equal weight. The Northeast has the largest average student discount in this sample, $9.08. The ranking is sensitive to which museums were included: Chicago is the only Midwestern city, and Houston and San Francisco each contribute just one museum. I therefore interpret it as a comparison of the collected prices, rather than an estimate of the discount a typical student would find across each region.

title: What Is Your Student ID Worth?
section: A larger discount can still mean a larger bill
text:
A larger discount can still mean a larger bill



Adult and student admission prices at all eighteen museums. Six museums charge neither group for general admission.


The Getty Center and Hammer charge neither group for general admission. Their student-ID saving is zero, yet they are inexpensive choices. The Getty requires a timed reservation; Hammer does not require one for individual visits. Free admission does not remove parking costs or guarantee unrestricted access.
Eligibility changes the story too. At the Whitney, visitors 25 and under enter free regardless of enrollment. Switching both comparison groups to age 22 reduces New York’s mean student-ID saving from $9.50 to $6.50. Crediting the entire adult ticket to student status would exaggerate the card’s value.
The MCA Chicago has posted online prices and in-person pay-what-you-can admission. Its listed discount is not a guaranteed reduction in what someone must pay. Excluding MCA gives Chicago a mean saving of $3.00. Restricting the comparison to museums with positive adult prices also changes Boston’s mean from $5.00 to $7.50. The paid-only average answers how much students save at museums that charge admission; including free museums describes the saving across the full sampled set. The choice depends on which visits the reader is considering.

section: Plan around eligibility, then the calendar
text:
Plan around eligibility, then the calendar
My practical rule: choose the museums first, check age and student eligibility second, then compare free hours. Woodmere offers free Sundays, while ICA Boston’s free Thursday evenings require advance tickets. These are calendar savings available beyond students. Keep pay-what-you-wish separate from guaranteed free admission, and confirm hours at the official links before traveling.

title: How Lisa Wins at Every Distance and Still Loses
text:
Lisa is more accurate than Bart at every distance. So how does Bart finish with the higher success rate?

At the Springfield carnival, Homer declares Bart the ring-toss champion: he lands 77% of his shots, against Lisa’s 63%. Lisa objects. She did better from both the near line and the far line. Surely winning in every category means winning overall?
Lisa’s argument leaves out how often each player throws from each distance. Comparing their overall success rates also compares the difficulty of the shots they took. In this example, that difference is large enough to reverse the ranking—a pattern known as Simpson’s paradox. The name refers to statistician Edward H. Simpson, whose 1951 paper examined the interpretation of grouped data. The cartoon family is our teaching cast.






Figure 1: Different mixes, different winners. This AI-generated teaching comic depicts Lisa, Bart, and Homer Simpson in a fictional classroom example; it is not a scene from the television series.





Suppose each sibling takes 100 shots. Lisa chooses mostly the harder, far-distance throws; Bart mostly the easier, near-distance ones. Here are the invented teaching data, with successes divided by attempts:








Distance
Lisa: successes / attempts (rate)
Bart: successes / attempts (rate)




Near/easier

72 / 90 (80%)


Far/harder
54 / 90 (60%)
5 / 10 (50%)


Overall
63 / 100 (63%)
77 / 100 (77%)



Fictional teaching data. Overall rates use total successes divided by total attempts, rather than an unweighted mean of the two rates.
Using a shared 50:50 mix of near and far attempts: Lisa 75%, Bart 65%. These standardized rates hold the observed group rates fixed; they are not causal estimates or predictions.
Lisa leads by 10 percentage points at each distance, yet Bart leads by 14 points overall. No observations disappeared. The grouped and overall comparisons use exactly the same observations.
The key is the denominator. Lisa’s impressive 90% near-shot rate describes only ten attempts. Her 60% far-shot rate describes ninety. Bart’s easier shots receive most of the weight in his overall rate; Lisa’s harder shots receive most of the weight in hers.



Think of the overall rate as a mixture. Each distance supplies a success rate; its share of attempts determines how much of that rate goes into the mixture:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{Lisa: }& 0.10\times90\%+0.90\times60\%=63\%\\
\text{Bart: }& 0.90\times80\%+0.10\times50\%=77\%.
\end{aligned}
\]
Each overall rate lies between that player’s two distance-specific rates. Lisa’s is pulled toward 60%; Bart’s toward 80%. Our intuition compares the rates but overlooks their different weights. Averaging the two percentages equally would describe a different mix of shots.

With any shared mix, Lisa retains her ten-point advantage: each ingredient in her average is ten points higher. The reversal needs different weights. Standardization makes the composition comparable, holding the observed rates fixed; it does not guarantee how either sibling would perform in another game.



For who landed a larger share of their actual throws, the overall scoreboard answers correctly: Bart. For who had the higher observed accuracy at the same distance, the grouped table answers: Lisa. Different questions justify different summaries.
The same problem can arise when comparing job-training programs. Suppose one program enrolls more people with little prior work experience. Its overall placement rate could be lower even if placement rates are higher within each experience group. The overall rate describes outcomes for the people actually enrolled; a comparison using a common experience mix answers a different question. Neither comparison, by itself, tells us how much the training helped participants.
But splitting data into groups is no automatic cure. To ask whether a program causes better outcomes, we need to understand how people enter it and which variables should be adjusted for. Grouping on a consequence of participation can even remove part of the effect we want to measure. As Pearl (2014) explains, causal interpretation requires knowledge of the process behind the data, beyond the table. Lisa’s table demonstrates an arithmetic reversal, not proof of innate skill or a causal effect.

Bart landed a larger share of the shots he actually took. Lisa had a higher success rate at each distance. Both statements are true because the players took different mixes of shots. If Homer wants to compare their observed accuracy on equal terms, he needs to use the same distance mix for both.



Data, sources, and reproduce it

All four counts are constructed for this explanation; they are not observations from a television episode or an empirical study. The comic was made with OpenAI’s built-in image generation tool and checked against the table. Its generation prompt is included.
Download the four-row dataset, Python reproduction script, calculated results, or replication instructions. Run the script with Python 3 from this post’s folder; it generates the table and results using the standard library. The interactive demonstration implements the same weighted averages in JavaScript. AI-generated artwork is supplied as an asset; rerunning the analysis does not regenerate it.

title: Why a Tech-Rich State Can Still Have a Wide Gender Pay Gap
text:
A lucrative career can carry a cost that never appears on a pay stub: control over one’s time.
That trade-off sits at the center of economist Claudia Goldin’s explanation for why gender earnings gaps persist. Jobs can reward long, inflexible hours disproportionately. When someone must also be available for a child or an aging parent, a household faces a costly choice over whose career bends. The consequences can accumulate even when partners begin with similar qualifications. Goldin received the 2023 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences for her research on women’s labor market outcomes.
Her work suggests a question for the modern technology economy. Does creating more well-paid technical work make a place more equal—or does equality depend on who gets those jobs and how careers are organized?
Five years of Census estimates—2019 and 2021–2024—give a complicated answer. Technology occupations offer high earnings for women and men. But tech’s expanding footprint has not brought a comparable increase in women’s representation. A state’s concentration of technical workers also says surprisingly little about either its current earnings gap or how much that gap narrowed.

title: Does a Richer, More Technical Economy Close the Gender Earnings Gap?
section: A dollar is not the same everywhere
text:
A dollar is not the same everywhere
The first map asks how much women earn for every $100 men earn, comparing median annual earnings among full-time, year-round workers age 16 and older. A value of $85 means women’s median is 15% below men’s. This compares two groups’ medians; it does not compare colleagues doing identical jobs.



Gender earnings ratios across 50 states. Darker green indicates a ratio closer to parity; each state’s women’s median is divided by its men’s median.


The highest point estimate is $91.4 in New York, followed by Vermont at $91.0. Louisiana and Utah are near $73.1 and $73.6, respectively. Women’s median earnings fall below men’s in every state. These are estimated rankings, not statistically established differences between neighboring ranks.
Smaller gaps appear in several Northeastern and Pacific states, while several Southern and Mountain states have larger gaps. The exceptions matter: a regional label cannot explain every state’s experience. Large land areas also dominate the map visually; they do not represent more workers or receive greater statistical weight.

title: Does a Richer, More Technical Economy Close the Gender Earnings Gap?
section: Technology hubs do not share one earnings pattern
text:
Technology hubs do not share one earnings pattern
The second map measures technology concentration as computer and mathematical occupations divided by all civilian employed residents age 16+. It covers workers across industries, including remote workers, rather than counting technology companies or measuring AI adoption.



Technology occupation concentration provides a second geography to compare with earnings parity. Read its percentage scale separately from the first map’s dollar ratio.


Washington and Maryland have almost identical technology shares, about 6.7% each. Yet women’s median earnings are 82.3% of men’s in Washington and 89.5% in Maryland. A similar concentration of technical work can coexist with quite different earnings gaps.



Each state is one dot. A higher position means a smaller gender earnings gap. Selected states are labeled with postal abbreviations.


Across states, the correlation between technology share and the earnings ratio is 0.28. This modest positive association leaves substantial variation unexplained. Technology employment may expand opportunity, but its presence does not tell us whether women enter those occupations, reach senior roles, or share their earnings gains.

title: Does a Richer, More Technical Economy Close the Gender Earnings Gap?
text:
Richer places, smaller gaps—with exceptions
Household income has a stronger positive association with the earnings ratio: 0.45 across states. Rank correlations preserve that ordering. Here, “richer” means higher median household income, not greater household wealth. Income is a flow; wealth is accumulated assets minus debts.



Higher household income is associated with a higher earnings ratio, but Utah illustrates why income alone is insufficient.


Utah’s median household income is $96,658, yet its earnings ratio is only 73.6%. New York’s household income is lower, at $85,820, while its ratio is much closer to parity. Nor does a smaller gap necessarily mean higher earnings: Vermont has a higher ratio than Washington, but lower median earnings for both women and men.

title: Does a Richer, More Technical Economy Close the Gender Earnings Gap?
section: Prosperity is only part of the story
text:
Prosperity is only part of the story
These comparisons describe residents, not causal effects or individual wage offers. Occupation, seniority, education, caregiving, and hours even within full-time work can affect the gap; this analysis does not separate their contributions or measure discrimination. Restricting the sample also leaves out part-time workers and people outside employment.
All correlations give each state equal weight. Census estimates already incorporate survey weights. Maps show point estimates; published margins of error are retained in the replication files, and small differences should not be overinterpreted. State averages conceal local and demographic differences.
The takeaway is that a prosperous, technical economy can still have a substantial gender earnings gap. Assessing economic opportunity requires looking at how earnings are distributed alongside how much income a place generates.

title: How Much of the Participation Decline Reflects an Aging Population?
text:
Note



BLOG 3 · THE PEOPLE BEHIND THE AVERAGE
Participation fell 0.54 percentage points. A shift toward older ages pulled it down; changes within age groups partly offset the decline.

title: How Much of the Participation Decline Reflects an Aging Population?
text:
Participation and population aging
A decline in labor-force participation can reflect changes in participation within age groups, changes in the population’s age distribution, or both. The distinction matters when interpreting the post-pandemic labor market: an older population can have a lower participation rate even if participation rises among younger adults. I use CPS data to measure how much each component contributes to the change between 2019 and 2024.
Using IPUMS CPS microdata, I compare 2019, before the pandemic, with 2024. The weighted annual participation rate fell from 63.40% to 62.86%. But that average combines two things: how likely people of each age are to participate, and how common each age group is.

title: How Much of the Participation Decline Reflects an Aging Population?
text:
Sample and weights
I use all twelve Basic Monthly CPS samples in each year: 2,611,419 person-month records, of which 2,115,648 meet the analysis criteria. The population is civilians age 16 or older with a valid labor-force status and positive weight. These are observations, not distinct people; the CPS interviews respondents in multiple months.
Every population statistic uses WTFINL, the final person weight. I calculate each month’s weighted participation rate, then average the twelve rates equally. Age shares and within-age rates use the same monthly-normalized weights, keeping the decomposition consistent. The code imports the matching DDI metadata so that the weight’s implied decimals are handled correctly.
Participation includes employed people and unemployed people in the labor force. It is not an employment rate. Someone outside the labor force is not automatically unemployed.

title: How Much of the Participation Decline Reflects an Aging Population?
text:
Compare people of similar ages
Figure 1 compares participation across age groups in each year. Adults aged 25–54 have substantially higher participation rates than those 65 and older. Between 2019 and 2024, participation rose in all five displayed groups below age 65: for ages 35–44, it increased from 83.33% to 84.77%. Among ages 65–74, it fell from 28.47% to 27.67%. These are comparisons of age groups in two years; they do not track the same people as they age.



Weighted participation rose in the five age groups below 65 and fell in the two older groups.

title: How Much of the Participation Decline Reflects an Aging Population?
text:
The changing age distribution
The national participation rate weights each age group’s participation rate by its population share. If groups with lower participation account for more of the population, the national rate can fall even with unchanged participation within every age group.
Figure 2 shows this compositional shift. Adults 65 and older increased from 20.40% to 22.23% of the weighted population. Because their participation rates are relatively low, that shift puts downward pressure on the national average. These are population shares estimated with weights, not percentages of downloaded rows.



The population shares of both older age groups increased between 2019 and 2024.

title: How Much of the Participation Decline Reflects an Aging Population?
text:
Separate the two changes
A symmetric Kitagawa decomposition splits the observed change into an age-composition component and a within-age participation component. It averages the two possible orders of changing shares and rates, so neither year gets special treatment.
Figure 3 gives the result: -0.98 percentage points from composition, offset by +0.44 points from within-age changes, producing the observed -0.54 points. The composition component is larger than the net decline because the two components move in opposite directions. A percentage point is a difference between rates, not a percent change.



Age composition contributes −0.98 percentage points, within-age participation +0.44, and the total is −0.54.


Using narrower, mostly five-year age groups gives −1.09 points for composition and +0.55 for within-age changes. The magnitudes change, but the interpretation survives.

title: How Much of the Participation Decline Reflects an Aging Population?
text:
What explains the aggregate decline?
In this decomposition, the shift in age composition contributes -0.98 percentage points, exceeding the observed 0.54-point decline. Within-age participation changes offset 0.44 points of that decline. The aggregate therefore understates the improvement within many age groups. These results help explain the national rate, but they do not tell us why participation changed within those groups.
This is descriptive accounting, not a causal estimate of aging or the pandemic. Within-age changes also reflect health, education, family circumstances, and other composition; even the oldest age bin contains aging. Estimates are not seasonally adjusted, population-control revisions can affect comparisons, and repeated respondents rule out treating all rows as independent. I make no significance claims or claims about individual retirement decisions.

title: More Tech, Better Jobs?
text:
Note



BLOG 4 · TECHNOLOGY AND LOCAL LABOR MARKETS
Tech employment share rose in 48 of 50 states between 2018 and 2024. That expansion did not come with a consistent improvement in broader employment outcomes.

title: More Tech, Better Jobs?
section: Tech employment and the wider labor market
text:
Tech employment and the wider labor market
Does a growing share of workers in computer and mathematical occupations go together with better employment outcomes for a state’s residents? Growth in these occupations could accompany stronger labor demand, but unemployment also depends on how labor supply and the rest of the economy change. A larger tech workforce alone does not settle the question.
I compare changes in occupational shares, unemployment, and employment/population ratios across all 50 states from 2018 to 2024, using six available years of ACS data. I then examine San Francisco and Santa Clara counties to see how these two parts of the Bay Area fit the national pattern.

title: More Tech, Better Jobs?
section: Measure what the data actually observe
text:
Measure what the data actually observe
The source is the Census Bureau’s American Community Survey (ACS) 1-year estimates, tables S2401 and S2301. I define tech concentration as the share of employed residents age 16 and older in computer and mathematical occupations. This transparent proxy captures an occupational mix—not technological sophistication, patents, all STEM work, or AI adoption.
Two outcomes describe the wider labor market: unemployment and the employment/population ratio. Lower unemployment is encouraging, but it can also reflect people leaving the labor force; a higher employment/population ratio provides a complementary perspective.
The panel covers 2018, 2019, and 2021–2024: 300 state-year observations, plus 12 county-year observations. DC is retained in the download but excluded from the 50-state comparisons. I start after the 2018 occupation-classification revision and omit 2020 because Census did not release standard 1-year estimates. Each state receives equal weight; published ACS estimates already use survey weights.

title: More Tech, Better Jobs?
text:
Where did tech employment expand?
Figure 1 ranks the ten states with the largest increases in tech employment share. Washington, Delaware and Texas lead this comparison. The broader shift was widespread: 48 of 50 states recorded an increase. This establishes where the occupational mix changed, but says nothing yet about whether employment conditions improved.



The ten largest increases in tech employment share, 2018–2024.

title: More Tech, Better Jobs?
text:
Follow the changes
Figure 2 subtracts each state’s 2018 value from its 2024 value. A one-point increase means, for example, moving from 3% to 4% tech employment—not a 1% increase in the number of tech workers.
In both panels, higher values on the vertical axis indicate improvement: lower unemployment in the first and a higher employment/population ratio in the second. Across states, larger increases in tech employment share are associated with less improvement in unemployment (r = −0.29). The correlation with employment/population improvement is close to zero (r = +0.04). The two measures provide little evidence of a consistent positive association over this period.
This is not simply California driving the pattern: excluding it gives correlations of −0.27 and +0.05, respectively. Rank correlations also preserve the broad interpretation. I checked the denominator, too: every state with a rising tech share also had an increase in its estimated number of tech workers. Their shares did not rise solely because other employment contracted.



Within-state changes reveal little connection with employment/population improvement.

title: More Tech, Better Jobs?
text:
Timing changes the story
For each period, Figure 3 ranks states by the change in tech employment share and compares the 13 states at each end of the ranking. Each bar is an equally weighted mean change in the relevant employment outcome. The middle 24 states are excluded from this particular comparison.
In 2018–2019, the faster-tech group improved more on both measures. In 2019–2021 it deteriorated more. During 2021–2024, unemployment fell 1.24 points in the faster-tech group versus 1.70 in the slower group, while employment/population gains were similar (1.80 versus 1.72 points). Faster tech growth did not bring a consistent advantage.
Groups change across periods; these are equal-weight descriptive averages, not matched comparisons. Periods also differ in length. The 2019–2021 interval spans the pandemic and cannot isolate its initial shock.



Faster and slower tech-growth groups do not show a consistent employment advantage across periods.

title: More Tech, Better Jobs?
section: San Francisco and Santa Clara counties
text:
San Francisco and Santa Clara counties
Santa Clara County’s tech share rose from 11.90% to 15.94%, while its ACS unemployment rate rose from 3.9% to 5.2%. San Francisco County also recorded increases in both. These fixed county boundaries offer a local comparison without treating California as the Bay Area; the two counties do not represent the full nine-county region.



From 2018 to 2024, tech employment share and unemployment both rose in the two counties.

title: More Tech, Better Jobs?
section: Put the changes on the map
text:
Put the changes on the map
The maps add a geographic view of the same 50-state comparison. Washington and Texas show relatively large tech-share gains, but their unemployment outcomes differ. California also gains tech share while its unemployment rate rises. The two patterns do not line up into a simple geography of technology-led improvement.



Changes in technology occupation share across all 50 states, 2018–2024.





Unemployment improvement across all 50 states over the same period.


Read each legend separately: the color scales differ because the measures have different ranges. Large states occupy more space, not more statistical weight. Boundaries come from the Census 2024 cartographic boundary files; state FIPS codes link geography to the analysis.

title: More Tech, Better Jobs?
text:
What the state comparisons show
Across these 50 states from 2018 to 2024, a larger increase in the share of residents working in computer and mathematical occupations was not consistently associated with better employment outcomes. The period comparisons also give mixed results. I would therefore treat growth in this occupational share as evidence of a changing employment mix; assessing the wider labor market still requires looking at unemployment and employment/population together.
These are descriptive associations, not causal effects. Migration, age structure, education, other industries and common shocks may influence both variables. ACS sampling error also matters, especially for counties and small changes; the download retains published margins of error, but the charts show point estimates and make no significance claims. Residence-based estimates—including remote workers—do not measure jobs located in local offices.

title: More Tech, Better Jobs?
text:
Sources and replication
Census ACS API: S2401 occupation counts and S2301 employment indicators; 2018 comparability guidance; 2020 release limitation. Data retrieved October 4, 2026. ACS rates are not interchangeable with the monthly BLS headline unemployment series.
Download the reproducibility package: source responses, analysis scripts, figures and README. No API key is included.

title: Why a Tech-Rich State Can Still Have a Wide Gender Pay Gap
section: First, look at where the gap is widest
text:
First, look at where the gap is widest
In Washington, a center of the technology economy, women working full time, year round had median annual earnings equal to 82.3 cents per dollar earned by men. In Maryland, another state with a similar concentration of technical workers, the figure was 89.5 cents.
The difference is substantial enough to challenge a simple story in which more technology jobs automatically produce equal outcomes.



How close are women’s median earnings to men’s? Darker green means a smaller gap.


Across the 50 states, women’s median earnings were below men’s everywhere. New York and Vermont had the highest point estimates, around 91.4 and 91.0 cents per dollar. Louisiana and Utah were near 73.1 and 73.6 cents. Small differences in these estimated rankings should not be treated as statistically established.
These figures compare the medians of women and men age 16 or older who worked full time, year round. They are earnings gaps, not evidence that a woman and a man doing the same job receive those different paychecks. Occupations, seniority, hours within full-time work, and self-employment can all differ. People working part time or outside paid work are not included.

title: Why a Tech-Rich State Can Still Have a Wide Gender Pay Gap
section: Is prosperity doing more of the work than technology?
text:
Is prosperity doing more of the work than technology?
Higher-income states generally have smaller gaps. Across states, the correlation between median household income and women’s earnings relative to men’s is 0.45. The correlation with technology concentration is weaker, 0.28. Here, technology means computer and mathematical occupations as a share of employed residents—not all employees of technology companies.



Prosperous states generally have smaller earnings gaps, but Utah is an important exception. Each dot represents a state.


The two features overlap: states with more technical workers also tend to have higher household incomes. To separate those patterns descriptively, I remove each variable’s linear relationship with household income and compare what remains. The technology–earnings-ratio correlation falls to -0.03, essentially zero.
That is a useful check on the original comparison, not proof that income explains the gap. Household income itself reflects earnings, household composition and other income sources. It is not an outside force randomly assigned to states. Nor is it wealth, which measures accumulated assets minus debts.
Utah illustrates the limits of prosperity as an explanation. Its median household income was $96,658, higher than New York’s $85,820, yet its earnings ratio was much lower. A high household income does not tell us whether two earners contribute equally to it.
The time comparison provides another test. Technology’s national employment share rose from 3.3% to 4.0%. Increases occurred in 48 of 50 states. Yet states with larger increases did not consistently see larger improvements in earnings parity: the correlation between those two changes is only 0.03. Rank correlation is also near zero.



The states gaining the most technology employment share were not consistently those with the largest narrowing of the earnings gap.


This separates a geographic pattern from a change over time. A tech-rich state can look different from a less technical state, yet expanding its technical workforce does not necessarily move its overall earnings ratio in the same direction. The comparison remains descriptive: migration and changes in other industries can affect both measures.

title: Why a Tech-Rich State Can Still Have a Wide Gender Pay Gap
text:
Who gets the technology jobs?
Nationally, women held 47.8% of all employed jobs, but only 26.9% of computer and mathematical jobs. Put another way, 2.2% of employed women worked in those occupations, compared with 5.5% of employed men.
The relevant question is therefore not only how many technical jobs a state has. It is whether women share in them.



Women’s share of technology occupations falls below their share of all employment in every state. Darker plum indicates a larger representation shortfall.


In Washington, women held 24.5% of technology occupations, compared with 46.9% of all employed jobs. Maryland’s corresponding shares were 32.5% and 49.8%. Utah’s tech workforce was only 19.8% women.
Over time, women’s national share of technical occupations was almost unchanged: 26.8% in 2019 and 26.9% in 2024, with lower estimates in between. The field grew, but its gender composition barely shifted between the endpoints. At the state level, women’s tech representation rose in 25 states and fell in the others.



Technology employment expanded, but women’s share of it ended almost where it began. The 2020 gap reflects the missing standard ACS release, as explained above.


That does not mean women gained no jobs. The estimated number of women in these occupations increased by 27.5%. Men also gained jobs, leaving the female share nearly flat. Expanding employment and changing who participates in it are different forms of progress.
This is consistent with an access problem: expanding a well-paid field may disproportionately benefit men when men fill most of its positions. But the data do not reveal whether the imbalance comes from education pathways, hiring, retention, caregiving constraints, workplace culture or other factors. It should not simply be labeled a difference in preferences.
And representation does not solve the entire geographic puzzle. Across all states, the correlation between women’s share of tech jobs and the overall earnings ratio is just 0.09. Accounting for household income raises it to 0.25, still a limited descriptive relationship. New York has a much smaller overall earnings gap than Washington, even though women are a minority of technical workers in both places.
The underrepresentation also persists in all 50 point estimates when I restrict the occupation counts to full-time, year-round workers. Nationally, women are 26.3% of that technical workforce, versus 44.0% of all full-time, year-round employed workers. Part-time employment alone does not account for the pattern.

title: Why a Tech-Rich State Can Still Have a Wide Gender Pay Gap
section: Does entering tech eliminate the gap?
text:
Does entering tech eliminate the gap?
It does not. But technology also should not be mistaken for a uniquely unequal field.
Nationally, full-time, year-round women in computer and mathematical occupations had median earnings of $95,158, compared with $111,053 for men. That is 85.7 cents per male dollar—a narrower gap than the 83.0 cents observed across all occupations using the same full-time, year-round civilian employed population.



Technology occupations pay more for both groups. They also retain a gender earnings gap. These are national medians for civilian employed residents, not averages of state medians.


The geographic contrast survives inside the broad category. In Washington, women’s median tech earnings were 84.2% of men’s; in Maryland, 90.3%. This still does not compare identical jobs. A software developer and a computer support specialist can share the same broad occupational label while earning very different amounts. Experience, management responsibilities and hours can differ too.
That distinction helps explain why both access and careers matter. More women entering a high-paying field could broaden opportunity. But entry alone need not equalize promotions, specialties, hours or pay. Conversely, a relatively small gap inside tech cannot determine a state’s overall gap: even in Washington, these occupations account for only 6.7% of employed residents. Most workers are elsewhere in the economy.
Nor can the overall median be decomposed into a weighted average of occupational medians. These comparisons identify patterns worth investigating; they do not calculate the fraction of the state gap caused by occupational sorting.

title: Why a Tech-Rich State Can Still Have a Wide Gender Pay Gap
section: What might actually narrow the gap?
text:
What might actually narrow the gap?
Goldin’s 2014 research points beyond the number of high-paying jobs to the price workers pay for flexibility. If earnings rise disproportionately with long or particular hours, reducing availability can carry a large career cost. Her analysis also found smaller adjusted gaps in technology and science than in business occupations. The lesson is about job design, not a claim that every technology job demands constant availability.
A concrete example comes from Goldin and Lawrence Katz’s research on pharmacy. They connect its evolution toward family-friendly, well-paid employment to changes in how the profession is organized. When qualified colleagues can substitute for one another, a worker’s absence need not interrupt the entire service. That makes flexibility less costly. Technology can help such coordination; its usefulness depends on how employers use it.
For technology employers, that suggests questions about shared project knowledge, reliable handoffs, promotion criteria and whether constant availability is being rewarded over performance. For access, the questions concern training, recruitment and retention. And the Nobel committee’s account of Goldin’s research highlights how parenthood can redirect earnings trajectories. Childcare and a more balanced division of care are relevant constraints to examine alongside workplace practices.
These are research-informed directions, not interventions evaluated by this state comparison. Testing them would require evidence on workers’ jobs, hours, experience and family circumstances over time. The maps cannot establish that childcare costs explain Utah or that flexible work explains Maryland.
Across 2019–2024, technical work expanded without a comparable shift in women’s share of it. States with faster tech growth did not consistently narrow their earnings gaps more. A technical economy can pay women well while employing relatively few of them, and a richer state can still have a wide gap. A credible strategy for equality has to ask both who enters the well-paid jobs and what makes it possible to build a career once there.

title: Why a Tech-Rich State Can Still Have a Wide Gender Pay Gap
text:
Data, sources and replication
Estimates use ACS 1-year data for 2019 and 2021–2024. The geographic levels, household-income comparisons and detailed earnings bars refer to 2024. B20017 measures the state map’s full-time, year-round earnings; B19013 measures household income; S2401 and B24010 measure technology concentration and representation among employed residents; B24020 checks full-time representation in 2024; B24022 supplies occupation earnings and the national earnings trend. Both lines in that trend use B24022’s civilian employed universe, which differs from B20017’s broader population with earnings. Full time means usually 35+ hours a week; year round means 50–52 weeks.
Only ratios, shares and counts are compared across years; annual dollar medians are not compared without inflation adjustment. The dollar bars and income scatterplot use 2024 dollars without geographic cost-of-living adjustment. The broad occupation definitions are verified against each year’s metadata. Changes in population controls, migration, employment selection and demographics still limit comparisons; no change is interpreted as an individual worker’s earnings gain.
The maps join Census state boundaries to estimates by FIPS code. State comparisons exclude DC and Puerto Rico and weight each state equally. The national results use the actual U.S. tabulation. Census estimates already use survey weights. Published margins of error are retained; charts show point estimates without significance claims. Sex is tabulated as male/female and does not describe all gender identities. Age, race, education and differences within states remain unadjusted.

title: Why a Tech-Rich State Can Still Have a Wide Gender Pay Gap
section: Did the gap at least narrow over time?
text:
Did the gap at least narrow over time?
Nationally, yes—but unevenly. Among full-time, year-round civilian employed residents, women’s median earnings across all occupations rose from 81.0 cents per male dollar in 2019 to 83.0 cents in 2024. In technology occupations, the ratio moved from 84.7 to 85.7 cents. Neither series shows steady progress at every observation.






NoteWhy is 2020 missing?



COVID-19 disrupted American Community Survey data collection, creating response problems and nonresponse bias. The resulting estimates did not meet Census’s quality standards, so it did not release the standard 2020 ACS one-year estimates. Census instead released experimental estimates using a different weighting approach. To keep this comparison consistent, the charts leave 2020 blank rather than mix those products or invent a value. Read the Census explanation.





National earnings ratios improved between the endpoints, but the intervening years show fluctuations. Both series use the same full-time, year-round civilian employed population definition.


Across states, 43 of 50 had a higher overall earnings-ratio point estimate in 2024 than in 2019. That is evidence of a broad descriptive improvement, not a finding that every measured change is statistically significant. These are repeated snapshots of residents, not the same workers followed through their careers.
The comparison spans the pandemic and changes in who was employed; it cannot isolate a technology effect from those changes.

title: Does One Year of Income Mislead Us About Mobility?
text:
Does averaging several income observations change how strongly parents’ income predicts their children’s earnings? In this tutorial, you’ll use SQL inside Python to link two generations and compare single-year and three-observation intergenerational elasticities (IGEs).
The IGE is the slope in:
\[\log(\text{child income})=\alpha+\beta\log(\text{parent income})+\varepsilon\]
A slope of 0.4 means 10% higher parental income is associated with roughly 4% higher child income. It measures relative persistence, not a causal effect or the chance of out-earning your parents.

section: 2. Match children to mothers with SELECT and JOIN
text:
2. Match children to mothers with SELECT and JOIN
Join people to itself, once as the child (c) and once as the mother (p):
SELECT c.id68 AS child_id68, c.pn AS child_pn, c.sex, c.weight,
       p.id68 AS parent_id68, p.pn AS parent_pn
FROM people AS c
JOIN parent_links AS l
  ON c.id68 = l.child_id68 AND c.pn = l.child_pn
 AND l.parent_type = 'birth_mother'
JOIN people AS p
  ON p.id68 = l.parent_id68 AND p.pn = l.parent_pn
WHERE c.birth_year BETWEEN 1970 AND 1974;

section: 3. Attach income, joining on wave and family
text:
3. Attach income, joining on wave and family
For each childhood interview (1981–83, about income years 1980–82), keep the family income only if the child and mother lived in the same family that year. Convert it to 2020 dollars with the BLS CPI-U for the income year:
SELECT pr.child_id68, pr.child_pn, f.income_year,
       f.total_income * (SELECT cpi FROM cpi WHERE year = 2020) / k.cpi AS real_income
FROM pairs AS pr
JOIN membership AS mc ON mc.id68 = pr.child_id68 AND mc.pn = pr.child_pn
                     AND mc.wave IN (1981, 1982, 1983) AND mc.current_member = 1
JOIN membership AS mp ON mp.id68 = pr.parent_id68 AND mp.pn = pr.parent_pn
                     AND mp.wave = mc.wave AND mp.family_id = mc.family_id
                     AND mp.current_member = 1
JOIN family_income AS f ON f.wave = mc.wave AND f.family_id = mc.family_id
JOIN cpi AS k ON k.year = f.income_year;
Children’s adult earnings observations cover income years 2000, 2002, 2004 and 2010, 2012, 2014. A CASE expression selects the reference-person or spouse earnings field according to each person’s role that year.

This extract combines reference-person total labor income with spouse labor income excluding farm and business income. Those definitions differ. The estimates below illustrate the matching and measurement workflow; they are not a like-for-like test of daughters’ versus sons’ total earnings persistence. A change in household role can also change the earnings coverage for the same person. Before drawing a substantive gender or age comparison, construct comparable earnings measures across roles and years and rerun the analysis. The README lists the fields used here.

4. Aggregate first with GROUP BY
Each child now has three parent years and three adult years. Joining them directly pairs every year with every other: on the real data, 4,554 rows for 506 children, nine each. Collapse each generation to one row per child first:
SELECT child_id68, child_pn,
       AVG(real_income) AS parent_mean,
       MAX(CASE WHEN income_year = 1981 THEN real_income END) AS parent_single
FROM parent_history
GROUP BY child_id68, child_pn
HAVING COUNT(real_income) = 3;
GROUP BY makes one group per child. The aggregate AVG collapses the group to its mean, and MAX(CASE ...) pulls out the 1981 value. HAVING filters groups, keeping children with all three years. The same query on 2010, 2012 and 2014 gives child_mean and child_single (2012). Joining the two summaries leaves one row per child.

title: Match Parents and Children with SQL in Python
section: 5. Estimate the IGE: one year vs. three
text:
5. Estimate the IGE: one year vs. three
Fit a weighted log–log regression on the same children with each income measure (full code with standard errors clustered by mother in 04_estimate.py). The function below calculates its slope with an intercept:
def fit_ige(d, child_col, parent_col):
    y = np.log(d[child_col]); x = np.log(d[parent_col]); w = d["weight"]
    xm, ym = np.average(x, weights=w), np.average(y, weights=w)
    return np.sum(w * (x - xm) * (y - ym)) / np.sum(w * (x - xm) ** 2)

Averaging raises the point estimate for daughters (0.12 → 0.21) and slightly for all children (0.35 → 0.37), but lowers it for sons (0.56 → 0.51). All three bootstrap intervals for the change include zero, so these data do not establish a change from averaging. The estimates also retain the earnings-coverage limitation above.
Why averaging can help. Annual income includes persistent differences and temporary fluctuations. The unweighted correlation of log parental family income in 1980 and 1982 is 0.81 among retained children with positive values in both years. Under a classical measurement-error model, temporary noise in parental income attenuates the slope; averaging can reduce that noise. It does not remove all measurement error or guarantee a higher IGE. The data contain an extreme case: one son’s family income for 1980 and 1981 is PSID’s $1 code, meaning “$1 or less, including zero and negative.” Read it as a real $1 income, and that one family moves the sons’ single-year IGE from 0.56 to 0.21. The averaged IGE rounds to 0.51 under both treatments in this particular sensitivity check. That is not a general guarantee that averaging removes an influential observation.

title: Match Parents and Children with SQL in Python
text:
6. Watch for life-cycle bias
Averaging can reduce temporary noise, but it does not resolve timing. If earnings trajectories differ by parental background, an early-career snapshot may misrepresent the relationship at mature ages. Follow the same 293 children with positive earnings in all six observed years, holding parental income and weights fixed:

Sons’ point estimate is 0.40 at average age 28 and 0.71 at 42; daughters’ corresponding estimates are 0.42 and 0.39. These are descriptive age-and-year comparisons, not identification of life-cycle bias alone: period conditions, earnings coverage, and selection into positive earnings may also matter. In the separate three-observation-window comparison, the sons’ age-40-minus-age-30 change has a 95% bootstrap interval spanning zero.
In the main sample, daughters’ averaged point estimate is 0.30 below sons’, but the difference’s 95% bootstrap interval is -0.67 to 0.03, which includes zero. We cannot conclude a gender difference from these estimates, or attribute the pattern to caregiving, hours, or participation without examining those mechanisms. Final-wave weights do not fully correct the additional selection from requiring linked income histories, and the mother-clustered intervals do not implement the full survey design.

Takeaways

SQL makes the match explicit. Join on the two-part person key, join family data on wave and family_id, and GROUP BY before joining generations.
One year can be a noisy snapshot. Averaging can improve the measure of long-run resources, but a short average remains imperfect and need not increase the estimated slope.
Check timing and comparability. Estimates vary across observed ages and years. Wide intervals, selective samples, and inconsistent earnings coverage limit what these comparisons establish.

Try it: inspect how the single-year estimate changes when you average parental income alone (Parent averaged only in results/ige_results.csv). This holds children’s earnings fixed and separates that change from averaging both generations.

3. Attach income by year
Join each child’s membership to the mother’s membership on the same wave and family_id. Require both to be current members. Then join family income on those same keys. The executable query is in 02_match.sql.
Parental resources are family income in 1980–1982, reported in interviews 1981–1983. Adult earnings are from 2010, 2012, and 2014, reported the following years. These adult observations span five calendar years, not three consecutive years.

title: Which College Majors Come Closest to Earnings Parity?
text:
Journalism appears to offer an encouraging answer to the gender earnings gap: women and men have the same estimated median, about $86,300, in this analysis of 2024 Census data. But here is the catch: only 4.5% of the included journalism graduates report an occupation as a news analyst, reporter, or journalist.
That changes what the finding means. We are comparing people who studied journalism, not equal pay inside newsrooms. Which majors come closest to parity remains an interesting question—but understanding the answer requires looking beyond the degree label.

title: Which College Majors Come Closest to Earnings Parity?
section: A major is a starting point, not a job
text:
A major is a starting point, not a job
Economists Carolyn Sloane, Erik Hurst, and Dan Black (2021) identify two stages of sorting: women and men enter different majors, then enter different occupations within the same major. Their evidence shows that accounting for undergraduate specialization and subsequent occupational destinations matters for understanding graduate earnings gaps.
This offers a more useful lens than assuming a small gap identifies a uniquely fair profession. A major’s median combines many career destinations. Equal group medians could coexist with unequal outcomes in particular jobs; unequal medians need not mean unequal pay for identical work.

title: Which College Majors Come Closest to Earnings Parity?
section: Explore the careers behind the estimates
text:
Explore the careers behind the estimates
Compare gaps shows labeled majors and their 90% intervals, ten at a time. Filter by family, change the ordering, or click a dot to select a major. Then switch to Pay & hours or Career destinations without changing the selected workers. The question buttons open the examples below directly. All three views belong to one linked explorer.

Open the interactive chart · Download estimates
Across 129 sufficiently sampled majors, journalism and miscellaneous engineering have equal estimated medians. Journalism’s ratio interval is approximately 95–105 cents per male dollar; miscellaneous engineering’s is 85–115 cents. Neither establishes a statistically definitive winner.
Open “Does journalism mean journalist?”. Its most common recorded occupations are marketing managers for women and “other managers” for men, each accounting for only a small share. The graduates are dispersed across jobs. The parity finding describes that mixture; it does not show why the medians coincide.

title: Which College Majors Come Closest to Earnings Parity?
section: Full time does not mean the same working life
text:
Full time does not mean the same working life
Claudia Goldin (2014) points to the organization of work: some jobs disproportionately reward long or particular hours. When continuous availability is valuable, workers who need flexibility can face a larger earnings penalty. This is a theory about compensation and job design, not simply a claim that women need different degrees.
Open “Does full time mean equal hours?” to inspect Finance. Women’s median is about 81 cents per male dollar. Even within this full-time, year-round sample, men report 45.2 usual weekly hours, versus 43.5 for women. “Full time” has not equalized hours. That descriptive difference does not measure how much of the earnings gap hours explain, or establish a flexibility penalty.
A concrete example of the job-design mechanism comes from Goldin and Lawrence Katz’s pharmacy research (2016). They link changes making pharmacists more substitutable—including organizational and technological changes—to smaller penalties for part-time work. Their evidence concerns pharmacists, not every person with a pharmacy degree. It illustrates why the jobs a major leads to can matter alongside the major itself.

title: Which College Majors Come Closest to Earnings Parity?
text:
What the chart can establish
Earnings, representation, occupations, and hours all use the same workers: U.S. residents ages 25–64, BA or higher, classified as private/government employees, with positive wage/salary income, 35+ usual weekly hours, and 50+ weeks worked. Earnings are in 2024 dollars; the first bachelor’s major is used. Occupation describes the current or most recent job, not every job contributing to annual income.
Census person weights produce medians, shares, and mean hours; 80 replicate weights produce earnings-ratio intervals. Each major needs 100 sampled women and 100 sampled men; 45 smaller categories are omitted. Intervals are pointwise, not adjusted for ranking many majors. The README documents the unavailable General Business interval.
The takeaway: journalism graduates’ apparent parity is not evidence of equal pay in journalism. The economic question is how a degree maps into jobs and how those jobs reward time. Research identifies those mechanisms; this chart lets you inspect career composition and hours, but cannot identify their causal contributions. Age, experience, graduate education, discrimination, and other unmeasured differences remain possible influences.
Sources: 2024 ACS PUMS; papers linked above. Sex is recorded male/female. Code, definitions, and replication files.

text:
What does the card actually save?
You have chosen a museum. Is it worth finding your student ID before leaving home? To answer that practical question, I used R’s rvest package to collect official admission information for 18 museums across eight U.S. cities. The comparison holds the visit and visitor’s age constant: what does a student pay, compared with an otherwise equivalent nonstudent?
That distinction matters. A museum that admits everyone free offers no extra student discount. A youth ticket available to nonstudents is not a benefit of enrollment. I therefore measure student-ID saving as the adult price minus the student price at the same age.
The baseline is a 30-year-old, nonresident, full-time college student with valid ID. Age 30 separates student eligibility from youth offers; the explorer also compares 22-year-olds. School partnerships, residency benefits, memberships, fees, parking, and separately ticketed exhibitions are excluded.

title: How Much of the Participation Decline Reflects an Aging Population?
section: Can participation improve while the national rate falls?
text:
Can participation improve while the national rate falls?
Can population aging explain falling participation despite gains among younger adults? In IPUMS CPS data, weighted participation fell from 63.40% to 62.86% between 2019 and 2024. Participation includes working people and unemployed jobseekers, unlike an employment rate.

title: How Much of the Participation Decline Reflects an Aging Population?
section: Compare like ages, then count their shares
text:
Compare like ages, then count their shares
Figure 1 shows participation rising in all five displayed age groups below 65. For ages 35–44, it increased from 83.33% to 84.77%. Among ages 65–74, it fell from 28.47% to 27.67%. These comparisons do not follow the same people as they age.



Weighted participation rose in the five age groups below 65 and fell in the two older groups.


Figure 2 shows adults 65 and older growing from 20.40% to 22.23% of the weighted population. Moving population weight toward groups with lower participation can pull down the average, even without any change in their participation rates.



The population shares of both older age groups increased between 2019 and 2024.

title: How Much of the Participation Decline Reflects an Aging Population?
section: How the decomposition separates the changes
text:
How the decomposition separates the changes
The idea is to separate who makes up the population from how likely people of each age are to work or look for work. The method is called a symmetric Kitagawa decomposition.
Start with an imaginary population of 100 adults: 60 younger and 40 older. If 80% of the younger group and 20% of the older group participate, there are \(60\times0.80+40\times0.20=56\) participants. The overall rate is 56%.
The first formula expresses that same calculation:
\[
P_t=\sum_g s_{g,t}p_{g,t}.
\]
Read it as “multiply each group’s share of the population by its participation rate, then add the answers.” The symbols are shorthand:

\(P\): the overall participation rate; \(s\): a group’s population share; \(p\): its participation rate.
\(g\): the age group; \(t\): the year. The subscripts are labels, not multiplication.
\(\sum_g\): “add up all age groups.” Write 60% as 0.60 when calculating.

Now imagine the population becomes 50 younger and 50 older adults, with both groups’ participation rates unchanged. The total becomes \(50\times0.80+50\times0.20=50\) participants. Participation falls from 56% to 50% entirely because the age mix changed. Nobody in either group became less likely to participate.
In the real data, both shares and participation rates change. The next formulas separate their contributions. Here \(0\) means 2019, \(1\) means 2024, and \(\Delta\) means “change”:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Delta P &= P_1-P_0=C+W,\\[4pt]
C &= \sum_g(s_{g,1}-s_{g,0})\frac{p_{g,1}+p_{g,0}}{2},\\[4pt]
W &= \sum_g(p_{g,1}-p_{g,0})\frac{s_{g,1}+s_{g,0}}{2}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Read \(C\) as “the age-mix contribution.” For each group, subtract its old share from its new share, multiply by its average participation rate across the two years, then add across groups. In our imaginary example, \(C\) is −6 percentage points.
Read \(W\) as “the participation-within-groups contribution.” For each group, subtract its old participation rate from its new rate, multiply by its average population share, then add. In our example, \(W\) is zero because neither group’s participation rate changed.
Each fraction adds the two years’ values and divides by two: an ordinary average. Using both years is what makes the method symmetric, rather than favoring one reference year. The contributions add exactly to the overall change. Multiply the formula’s results by 100 for percentage points: moving from 56% to 50% is a fall of six points.
In the CPS results, ages 35–44 contribute +0.23 points to \(W\): their participation increase is multiplied by their average population share. Figure 3 adds contributions from all seven age groups.

title: How Much of the Participation Decline Reflects an Aging Population?
text:
What the components reveal



Age composition lowers participation, while within-age changes partly offset the decline. Their sum equals the observed total.


Figure 3 adds the components: -0.98 + 0.44 = -0.54 percentage points. Changes in age composition outweigh the decline; within-age gains partly offset them. Narrower age bins give the same interpretation.
The economic intuition is that participation falls at retirement ages. Aaronson and colleagues (2014) distinguish population aging from participation declines associated with weak demand for workers. Montes, Smith, and Dajon (2022) distinguish aging from unusually early pandemic retirements. This age-only decomposition cannot identify those individual retirement decisions.
Judge recovery using age-group participation alongside the headline rate. Returning to 2019’s overall rate is a different benchmark when the population is older. The headline decline alone does not establish widespread withdrawal from work or reveal why participation changed.

Data and reproduction
I use twelve Basic Monthly CPS samples per year: 2,115,648 eligible person-month observations of civilians age 16+. Respondents can appear repeatedly.
All estimates use WTFINL person weights, normalized so each month contributes equally. Group shares and rates use consistent weights. Results are not seasonally adjusted; population-control revisions can affect comparisons. No significance claims are made.
Source: IPUMS CPS Version 13.0, University of Minnesota; Basic Monthly samples, 2019 and 2024. Method: Kitagawa (1955).
